content: Rachel Wilson contributed editorial support to the document. Approximately 2% of children aged 1 to 5 years, equating to about 434,000 children, have elevated blood lead levels (BLLs). Research indicates that these elevated BLLs are primarily caused by exposure to lead from deteriorating paint, interior settled dust, and exterior soil and dust in and around older, deteriorating housing. Renovation activities in older housing can also generate significant lead hazards unless proper dust containment and thorough cleaning are implemented. While children can be exposed to lead from various sources, the recommendations in this report focus on preventing childhood exposure to lead-based paint hazards in and around housing. The Advisory Committee on Childhood Lead Poisoning Prevention (ACCLPP) supports the principle of local and state decision-making to determine the most appropriate blood lead screening approach based on local conditions and data, as outlined in the revised 1997 guidelines. Ensuring that the healthcare system incorporates these guidelines is of critical importance. Follow-up care for children with elevated BLLs includes education on lead hazards, behavioral changes to reduce exposure, medical and developmental follow-up, nutritional recommendations, and environmental interventions. However, environmental interventions to control identified lead hazards and prevent further exposure may not always be implemented due to resource limitations or lack of statutory authority. Evidence suggests that the benefits of secondary prevention are limited, but identifying and providing services to children with elevated BLLs remain essential components of a comprehensive lead poisoning prevention program. To successfully eliminate elevated BLLs in children, programs must prioritize preventing lead exposure through housing-based primary prevention rather than relying solely on screening and secondary prevention. The actions recommended in this report can be undertaken by various entities, including health departments, public agencies, community-based organizations, and the private sector. Health departments must take a leadership role in fostering collaboration among housing agencies, elected officials, and other stakeholders. Recent advancements in technology and national housing policy can aid in addressing unsafe housing, which is the primary vector of lead exposure. This document provides a rationale for emphasizing primary prevention and outlines a comprehensive program based on eight core elements. Specific examples of recommended program elements are documented through a CDC-funded project titled Building Blocks for Primary Prevention: Protecting Children from Lead-Based Paint Hazards, initiated in October 2002. Even with the most intensive primary prevention efforts to increase the supply of lead-safe housing, achieving this goal will take years. Therefore, childhood lead poisoning prevention programs (CLPPPs) should supplement systemic housing-based primary prevention changes with fast-track initiatives to identify high-risk families who could benefit from immediate assessment and risk-reduction services to prevent further childhood lead exposure. As the focus shifts toward primary prevention, program evaluation efforts should become a research priority to ensure that future resource commitments are directed toward cost-effectively achieving program and national goals to reduce childhood lead exposure. Members of the ACCLPP emphasize that primary prevention through the removal of ongoing lead exposure sources should be promoted as the most effective means of preventing elevated BLLs. Strong support and resource allocation from the federal government will increase the likelihood of success for state and local initiatives. Federal agencies play a crucial role in supporting primary prevention programs by sponsoring research, developing tools and guidance for assessing and monitoring lead safety in housing, enforcing lead-safe practices in federally supported housing programs, funding lead hazard control and evaluation programs, providing technical assistance, and updating regulations to align with primary prevention goals. The ACCLPP recommends that the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) strengthen its efforts to promote and facilitate primary prevention and maintain a leadership role in collaboration with other federal agencies. This guideline provides a framework for developing and implementing a primary prevention strategy, along with references and resources to achieve this goal. Childhood lead exposure remains a significant public health problem, adversely affecting cognitive and behavioral development. Elevated BLLs in children are associated with growth impairment, increased blood pressure, impaired heme synthesis, hearing threshold increases, and slowed nerve conduction. Lead toxicity also has economic implications, as cognitive ability is strongly correlated with productivity and lifetime earnings. An increase of 10 µg/dL in a child’s BLL may reduce their lifetime earnings by approximately $37,000. A national survey found that children at the highest risk for elevated BLLs are those living in metropolitan areas, in housing built before 1946, from low-income families, and of African-American or Hispanic origin. Lead exposure disproportionately affects children in low-income families living in older housing, contributing to social disparities in health, education, and quality of life. Intervening after a child’s BLL becomes elevated may reduce or prevent further lead exposure but does little to reverse lead-associated cognitive impairment. Most CLPPPs rely on routine blood lead screening to identify children with elevated BLLs. However, follow-up care for children with BLLs of 10–20 µg/dL typically includes education, behavioral changes, medical and developmental follow-up, nutritional recommendations, and environmental interventions. Children with BLLs ≥15 µg/dL generally receive more intensive follow-up services as BLLs increase. Environmental interventions to control identified lead hazards and prevent further exposure are sometimes not carried out. The benefits of secondary prevention, even with comprehensive follow-up care, may be limited. Delaying corrective action until after exposure forces children to experience the harmful effects of lead. Even after corrective actions, reducing elevated BLLs is challenging due to the body burden of lead. Recent advancements in technology and national housing policy make the implementation of housing-based primary prevention feasible on a larger scale. These advancements include increased focus on low-income urban areas, data mapping techniques to identify high-risk neighborhoods, expanded knowledge about lead hazard control, and the development of low-cost tools for lead dust testing. The ACCLPP emphasizes the need for a concerted effort to implement housing-based primary prevention of childhood lead exposure. Collaboration among housing, community development, and code enforcement agencies, elected officials, federal agencies, property owners, and community-based organizations is essential. Expanding effective primary prevention initiatives will reduce the need for and increase the efficiency of secondary prevention services.
